tune
psnr, ssim, grain, zero-latency, fast-decode, animation (default none) - grain keeps film noise, animation cel art
Tuning & Profile

Tune adjusts the preset's settings towards a kind of source or a delivery constraint. grain raises the psy settings and loosens deblocking and adaptive quantisation so film noise survives rather than being smoothed into patches. animation goes the other way, suiting flat cel artwork with strong AQ and more B-frames.

fast-decode removes tools that cost the decoder, for weak playback hardware. zero-latency disables lookahead and frame reordering for live use.

psnr and ssim disable the psychovisual optimisations, which raises those scores and makes the picture look worse. They are benchmarking aids, not delivery settings.

grain|Grainy film scans; the most commonly used tune in x265.
animation|Cel animation and flat 2D artwork.
zero-latency|Live streaming, at a compression cost.
fast-decode|Playback on weak hardware.
ssim|Metric benchmarking only; visibly softer output.
profile
main, main10, main444-10, main12, the -intra variants and more - Caps tools so a target decoder accepts the stream
Tuning & Profile

Restricts the encoder to the coding tools and bit depths a given HEVC profile permits, so a decoder implementing only that profile can play the result. main is 8-bit 4:2:0, main10 is 10-bit 4:2:0, and the 444 and 12-bit variants cover higher chroma and precision.

main10 is worth knowing about: 10-bit encoding reduces banding and usually compresses slightly better even from an 8-bit source, and unlike H.264 it is widely supported by hardware.

The -intra variants code every frame as a keyframe, for editing and mastering rather than delivery.

main|8-bit 4:2:0; the broadest hardware compatibility.
main10|10-bit 4:2:0; better gradients and widely supported.
main444-10|10-bit 4:4:4 for mastering or screen content.
main-intra|All-intra output for editing workflows.
level-idc
0 for auto or a level like 4.1 or 51 (default 0) - Constrains the stream for hardware, forces VBV in CRF
Tuning & Profile

The HEVC level written into the stream, bounding resolution, frame rate, bitrate and buffering so a decoder can tell in advance whether it can cope. Written either as a level number like 4.1 or as the integer form, 41.

Leave it at 0 and x265 works out a level from the encode. Set it when a specific hardware target demands one.

Setting it has a side effect worth knowing: it enables VBV in CRF mode, applying that level's rate and buffer limits. That constrains the bitrate on difficult scenes in a way plain CRF does not, so the file will no longer be constant quality.

0|The default; x265 derives the level from the encode.
4.1|A common hardware ceiling for 1080p.
5.1|4K delivery to modern decoders.
5.0|4K30 within tighter limits than 5.1.
deblock
tC:Beta offsets, each -6 to 6 (default 0:0) - Deblocking strength; raise to hide blocking, lower to keep detail
Tuning & Profile

Offsets for the in-loop deblocking filter, which smooths coded block edges before the frame is reused as a reference. The first number shifts the filter's strength, the second the threshold for treating an edge as worth filtering.

Negative values filter less, so grain and fine detail survive the loop rather than being averaged away, at the cost of visible block edges when the bitrate is short. Positive values smooth harder, which hides blocking at low rates and costs texture.

tune grain already loosens these, so an explicit setting replaces its choice.

0:0|The default, neutral filtering.
-1:-1|A mild sharpening for detailed live action.
-3:-3|Strong grain retention; needs bitrate behind it.
1:1|More smoothing, for low bitrate encodes that block.
bframes
0-16 (default 4) - Longest run of consecutive B-frames; raise for static scenes, 0 for low-latency output
Frames & Motion

The longest run of consecutive B-frames allowed. B-frames predict from both directions and are much cheaper to code than P-frames, so longer runs let static material spend its bits on the parts of the sequence that actually change.

Static scenes and animation gain the most. On busy live action the returns fall away past five or six, and no source gains much beyond eight.

Each B-frame adds reordering delay, so live and low-latency encoding sets this to 0 and accepts the efficiency loss.

4|The default, a sound balance.
8|Animation and static footage, where long runs pay.
0|Low-latency streaming; P and I frames only.
16|The maximum; realistically no better than 8.
ref
1-16 (default 3) - L0 reference frames the search may use; more helps repetitive motion, over 6 breaks conformance
Frames & Motion

How many L0 reference frames the motion search may predict from. More references help when content recurs - repetitive motion, cuts returning to an earlier shot, animation reusing artwork - because the encoder can point at a frame that genuinely matches.

Encoding time grows with each one and the gains fall off quickly on ordinary live action.

Compatibility is the real limit: HEVC levels bound the decoded picture buffer, and going past about six produces a stream many hardware decoders will refuse even though x265 encodes it happily.

3|The default, fine for general content.
5|Detailed or repetitive material, encoded offline.
1|Fastest, and the safest for constrained decoders.
6|About as high as is worth going before conformance suffers.
rc-lookahead
Above bframes, up to 250 (default 20) - Frames looked ahead for slice types; longer sharpens scenecuts and cutree
Frames & Motion

How many frames the encoder examines before fixing slice types and quantisers. The lookahead drives slice type decisions, scenecut detection and cutree, which spends bits on blocks that later frames will keep referring to.

A longer lookahead paces bits better across a scene and sharpens cuts, because the encoder can see a scene change coming rather than reacting after it. It costs memory and latency.

It must be larger than bframes to be useful, and past the length of a typical shot there is nothing further to learn.

20|The default.
40|Offline encoding, giving cutree more to work with.
60|Long takes and slow scenes.
10|Lower latency, at some rate control quality.
subme
0-7 (default 2) - Subpixel refinement passes in the motion search; higher costs speed but helps fine or fast motion
Frames & Motion

How hard the encoder refines motion vectors below whole-pixel precision, and how many candidates it tests while doing so. Higher values run more refinement passes and evaluate more positions.

The gain shows up on fine detail and fast motion, where a vector that is half a pixel out leaves a visible residual that has to be coded. On flat or slow content the extra passes find little.

It is one of the main speed dials the presets move, and the cost is roughly linear in the value.

2|The default, matching the medium preset.
4|Slower presets; a good offline compromise.
7|The maximum, for the last of the quality at a steep price.
0|Fastest, for real-time encoding.
merange
0-32767 (default 57) - Motion search range in pixels; raise past 57 only for fast pans at high resolution
Frames & Motion

The radius in pixels of the motion search. It bounds how far from the predicted position the encoder will look for a match, so it decides whether fast motion is found or coded expensively as intra blocks.

The default is generous for 1080p. Raising it helps whip pans, sports and high resolution material where genuine displacement between frames is large; on ordinary content the extra range goes unused and only costs time.

Values are capped below 32768, and search cost grows quickly, so large ranges are rarely worth it.

57|The default, ample for typical motion at 1080p.
92|Fast pans and sports at 4K.
32|Faster, adequate for slow or low resolution content.
16|Real-time encoding where search cost dominates.
aq-mode
0-4 (default 2) - Adaptive quantisation: 0 off, 1 plain, 2 auto-variance, 3 dark-scene bias, 4 edge aware
Quantization & Psychovisual

Adaptive quantisation redistributes bits within a frame, taking them from busy areas where quantisation error is masked and giving them to flat ones where banding and blocking show. Dark and smooth regions are where an HEVC encode visibly breaks down first, and this is the main defence.

Mode 1 distributes by block variance. Mode 2 adapts the strength using the frame's own content. Mode 3 adds a bias towards dark areas, and mode 4 weights by edge density, which helps keep flat regions next to sharp edges clean.

Switching it off raises metric scores and looks worse.

2|The default, auto-variance.
3|Dark and night scenes prone to banding.
4|Edge-aware; useful on animation and mixed content.
0|Off; better numbers, worse picture.
aq-strength
0.0-3.0 (default 1.0) - How strongly adaptive quantisation shifts QP; raise for flat gradients, lower if rates swing
Quantization & Psychovisual

How far adaptive quantisation may shift the quantiser between blocks. Higher values move more bits out of detailed areas and into flat ones.

Raise it when gradients, skies and fades show banding. Lower it on grainy or heavily textured sources, where a strong setting spends bits flattening the very noise the psy settings are trying to keep, and where it can make the bitrate swing between shots.

tune grain lowers this, so setting it explicitly replaces that choice.

1.0|The default, suitable for most content.
0.5|Grainy film, keeping bits on detail and steadying the rate.
1.3|Flat, clean sources such as animation that band easily.
0.0|Disables the redistribution.
psy-rd
0.0-5.0 (default 2.0) - Preserves the source's energy in the reconstruction; needs rd 3 or above, costs PSNR and SSIM
Quantization & Psychovisual

Psychovisual rate-distortion biases mode decisions towards preserving the source's energy rather than minimising measurable error, so the encoder stops preferring a smooth block over a detailed one that is slightly wrong. Without it x265 output tends to look plasticky, especially on faces and grain.

It costs PSNR and SSIM by design - it is choosing what those metrics score lower - which is why the psnr and ssim tunes set it to 0.

It needs rd 3 or higher to have any effect, since below that the encoder is not doing the rate-distortion analysis this modifies.

2.0|The default, and a good general setting.
1.0|Gentler, for clean digital sources.
4.0|Strong detail retention on grainy film.
0.0|Off, for metric benchmarking only.
psy-rdoq
0.0-50.0 (default 0.0, 1.0 on slow presets) - Favours higher energy through quantisation; needs rdoq-level 1 or 2
Quantization & Psychovisual

The quantisation-stage counterpart to psy-rd. Where psy-rd influences which mode is chosen, this biases which transform coefficients survive quantisation, favouring those that carry the source's high-frequency energy.

It is the more effective of the two for keeping film grain alive, and correspondingly the more expensive in bitrate. Values well above the default are normal on grain-heavy material.

It requires rdoq-level 1 or 2, which the faster presets do not enable, so on those it silently does nothing.

1.0|The slow-preset default; a reasonable starting point.
2.0|Noticeably stronger grain and texture retention.
10.0|Aggressive; used in grain-preservation setups at high bitrates.
0.0|Off, the default on faster presets.
rd
1-6 (default 3) - Rate-distortion optimisation level; higher looks harder and shrinks output, 4 aliases 3
Quantization & Psychovisual

How thoroughly the encoder analyses each block before committing to a coding decision. Higher levels test more possibilities with a fuller cost model instead of estimating, which shrinks the output at the same quality.

The scale is not fully granular: 4 behaves as 3 and 6 behaves as 5, so the meaningful steps are 1, 2, 3 and 5. Level 3 is where full rate-distortion optimisation begins, and it is also the point below which psy-rd stops working.

Cost rises sharply at 5, which is why only the slowest presets use it.

3|The default, and the minimum for psy-rd to function.
5|Slow presets; the last real quality step.
2|Faster, for time-constrained encodes.
1|Fastest, with visibly worse decisions.
qcomp
0.5-1.0 (default 0.6) - Quantiser curve compression; 1.0 behaves like constant QP, raise to favour busy scenes
Quantization & Psychovisual

Compresses the curve mapping frame complexity to quantiser, setting how bitrate is shared between easy and hard scenes. At 1.0 every frame gets the same quantiser, which is constant quality and lets size follow content. Lower values push frames towards equal size, giving complex scenes less than they need.

The default leans towards size predictability. Raising it gives busy scenes more bits and improves how the encode holds up on the hardest material, at the cost of a less predictable file size.

cutree uses this value too, so changes affect more than the scene-to-scene split.

0.6|The default.
0.7|A common adjustment for grain and detailed content.
0.8|Closer to constant quality across a wide difficulty range.
1.0|Constant quantiser behaviour.
master-display
G(x,y)B(x,y)R(x,y)WP(x,y)L(max,min) in SMPTE ST 2086 units, no default - Signals HDR10 mastering display volume
HDR Metadata

Signals the mastering display's colour volume for HDR10, in SMPTE ST 2086 form: the chromaticity of the green, blue and red primaries and the white point, then the display's maximum and minimum luminance. Coordinates are in units of 0.00002, and luminance in units of 0.0001 cd/m2.

This is metadata only. It does not change a single coded pixel - it tells the display what the content was graded on so it can tone-map sensibly to its own capabilities.

Take the values from the source's own metadata rather than inventing them; a wrong volume produces worse tone mapping than none.
max-cll
MaxCLL,MaxFALL in cd/m2, e.g. 1000,400, no default - Signals HDR10 content and frame-average light levels to displays
HDR Metadata

Two HDR10 light-level figures: the maximum content light level, which is the brightest single pixel anywhere in the video, and the maximum frame-average light level, the brightest frame taken as a whole. Both are in cd/m2.

Like master-display this is metadata and changes no pixels. Displays use it to decide how much tone mapping a title needs before it starts, rather than adapting scene by scene.

The values should be measured from the actual content - ffmpeg and mkvinfo can read them off a graded master - since guessed figures make displays tone-map for brightness that is not there.

1000,400|A typical 1000 cd/m2 grade.
4000,1000|A 4000 cd/m2 master.
0,0|Explicitly signals that the levels are unknown.
